title: Explain basic horse behaviour and body structure

lessons.title: How horses behave
lessons.html:
The horse is a prey animal

In nature, lions and other predators hunt horses and zebras. So the horse is always watching for danger. When it is scared, it wants to run away. If it cannot run, it may kick, bite or rear.

What this means for you

  • Move calmly and slowly around horses.
  • Speak softly before you come close, so the horse knows you are there.
  • Do not come from behind. The horse has a blind spot right behind it and right in front of its nose.
  • Always walk up to the shoulder.

Horses live in herds

Horses like to be with other horses. A horse alone can get stressed. In a herd, there is a leader, and some horses are higher in rank than others.

Body language

What you seeWhat it means
Ears forwardInterested, looking at something
Ears flat backAngry. Watch out for a bite or kick.
Ears turningListening
Head low, lip looseRelaxed
Eyes wide, white showingScared
Tail swishing hardAnnoyed or in pain
Hind leg liftedCould kick, or is resting
Snorting, head highAlarmed

Stay safe

  • Never stand directly behind a horse.
  • Never wrap the lead rope around your hand.
  • Wear closed shoes or boots.

lessons.title: Knowing the horse's body and markings
lessons.html:
Parts of the horse

You must know the names of the main parts of the horse so you can talk to your supervisor, the vet or the farrier.

  • Head: forehead, eyes, nostrils, muzzle, ears, poll (top of the head behind the ears).
  • Neck and mane.
  • Withers: the high point at the bottom of the mane. We measure the horse's height here, in hands.
  • Back, loins, croup and tail.
  • Shoulder, chest, belly and flank.
  • Legs: knee (front leg), hock (back leg), cannon, fetlock, pastern and hoof.

Colours

  • Bay: brown body with black mane, tail and lower legs.
  • Chestnut: red-brown all over, mane the same colour or lighter.
  • Black: all black.
  • Grey: white and black hairs; greys get lighter as they get older.
  • Dun, palomino and skewbald are other colours.

White markings

On the faceOn the legs
Star: white spot on the foreheadSock: white up to the fetlock
Stripe: narrow white line down the faceStocking: white up to the knee or hock
Blaze: wide white line down the faceCoronet: thin white ring above the hoof
Snip: white between the nostrils

Horses can also have a brand, a microchip or a passport. These help to prove who the horse is.

lessons.title: Is the horse healthy or sick?
lessons.html:
Check every horse every day

Look at each horse at least once in the morning and once in the afternoon. You are often the first person who sees that something is wrong.

Signs of a healthy horse

  • Alert, ears moving, interested in what is around it.
  • Eats and drinks well.
  • Shiny coat and bright, clear eyes.
  • Normal dung balls and clear or light yellow urine.
  • Stands evenly on all four feet and walks without limping.
  • Breathing slow and calm when resting.
  • Gums pink and wet.

Signs of a sick horse

  • Dull, head hanging, stands away from other horses.
  • Does not eat or drink.
  • Pawing, rolling, looking at its belly (colic).
  • Sweating when not working.
  • Runny nose, cough or fast breathing.
  • Limping or not wanting to put a foot down.
  • Wounds, swelling or heat in the legs.
  • No dung or very runny dung.
  • Very thin, ribs showing.

What to do

  1. Do not wait. Tell your supervisor straight away.
  2. Say what you saw: which horse, what signs, and when you saw them.
  3. Keep the horse calm and safe until help comes.
  4. Do not give any medicine unless the vet or your supervisor tells you to.

Key points

  • Horses are prey animals that run from danger.
  • Ears flat back mean an angry horse; keep away from the back end.
  • Know the parts, colours and markings of the horse.
  • Check every horse at least twice a day.
  • Tell your supervisor straight away if a horse looks sick.
